newsitem.title: UK: LME aluminium stocks fall over week, lead up.
newsitem.headline: LME aluminium stocks fall over week, lead up.

text.p: This week's London Metal Exchange (LME) stock returns featured aluminium which fell by nearly 19,000 tonnes to stand at 807,225 tonnes, down around 16.6 percent from a January 1997 peak of about 968,000 tonnes.
Lead stocks in LME warehouses rose by 4,775 tonnes over the week while copper declined by 7,275 tonnes.

Since the introduction of daily reporting on April 8 aluminium stocks have fallen by over 35,000 tonnes and traders noted most of the recent movement was from UK warehouses, while little found its way into LME warehouses globally.
With the unavailability of material in Rotterdam, interest has switched to most other European locations where warrants are being well bid for, Martin Squires of Rudolf Wolff.
We are expecting to see further good drawdowns of LME stocks in the coming days, Squires added.
Traders believed metal was been shipped to the U.S. and the Far East as consumers restocked.
U.S. Midwest physical traders are still looking for substantial shipments to arrive from Europe, broker GNI said in its commodity report.
Recently Angus MacMillan, analyst at brokers Billiton Metals, said the movement of material to the U.S. may reflect first quarter restocking by fabricators.
Historically the first two quarters of any given year see brisk demand for all base metals, which can spark declines in global stock levels.
But as summer approaches Northern hemisphere demand for primary aluminium drops as factories close for holidays and maintenance while production continues to flow.

MacMillan suggested the market would move into rough balance in the second half of 1997. Aluminiums outlook has not been improved by rumours that a number of producers on both sides of the Atlantic have been buying more petroleum coke than they require to maintain output at current levels.
The implications are clearly that they may be about to restart potlines mothballed as part of the MOU agreement, he said.
The MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) was a loose pact between major producing countries to restrict output in order to cut a huge surplus of the metal that built up in the early 1990s.
Good primary aluminium demand spread into the secondary sector. Total alloy stocks declined 1,780 tonnes over this week to 68,100 tonnes.
Slack physical demand saw lead stocks build by 4,775 to 114,475 tonnes.
Traders noted widespread deliveries into LME warehouses, believed to be of producer origin. It (stock) is arriving in most regions covered by the LME warehousing system, one trader said.
The trader noted fairly sizeable movements into Italy.
Physical demand took copper inventories down by 7,275 tonnes to 145,200 tonnes.

Tightness on nearby delivery dates for copper has seen spreads explode higher, analysts said. On Friday coppers cash to three months spread was around a $205 backwardation compared with a $70 backwardation last week.
Referring to the tight nearby backwardation an LME broker said "Low global stocks, tight physical markets and supply-side concerns are exacerbating the situation."
